messages.content: Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

A queue with workers suits variable, high-frequency work. A producer pushes jobs onto a queue (SQS, Redis, RabbitMQ) and a pool of workers pulls them off as capacity allows. This gives near-real-time processing, natural retries via dead-letter queues, and horizontal scaling — add workers and throughput rises. You manage broker infrastructure, handle idempotency for retried jobs, and watch for backlog growth if workers fall behind producers.

Scheduled batch runs suit predictable, periodic work — nightly reports, data syncs, cleanup tasks. A cron trigger fires a job on a fixed interval, processes a bounded chunk of data, then exits. No broker, no long-running worker fleet, and failures show up as a single run rather than scattered across a queue. Work waits for the next scheduled slot, and batches can grow unwieldy if data volume spikes between runs.

Most teams run both: a queue for user-triggered, latency-sensitive events, and batch jobs for aggregate or maintenance work where a few minutes' delay is fine. Choose a queue if jobs are bursty and need fast turnaround. Choose a scheduled batch if work is inherently periodic and volume is predictable — it's simpler to build and cheaper to run.
Add a paragraph on what happens when a job fails in each.

When a queued job fails, the worker retries it a few times with backoff, then routes it to a dead-letter queue if it keeps failing. The failure stays contained to that one job — other jobs in the queue keep processing normally, and nothing blocks. Someone (or an alert) has to notice the dead-letter queue and reprocess or discard the job manually, but the system as a whole degrades gracefully.

When a scheduled batch run fails, the whole run usually fails as a unit, since it's one process working through a bounded dataset. Partial completion is common, and it's messy — some records processed, some didn't, and figuring out where it stopped takes extra bookkeeping (checkpoints or idempotent re-runs). Recovery generally means re-triggering the same run, either manually or waiting for the next schedule, which can leave a gap where the data is stale until someone intervenes.
Add a recommendation for a small team.

output: For a small team, use a queue for anything a user waits on, and cron for everything else. Managed queue services (SQS, Cloud Tasks) need little setup, so the operational cost of adding a queue is low, and the payoff — no dropped signups, no stuck emails — is high. Reserve batch jobs for work that's genuinely periodic and low-stakes if delayed: reports, cleanup, syncs. Don't build a queue for things that fit fine in a nightly cron, and don't force user-facing work through a scheduled job just to avoid running a worker.
